name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Ragozin
summary: The Queen's Gambit Declined: Ragozin fuses a solid QGD centre with a Nimzo-Indian bishop pin for active, fully sound counterplay.
intro: The Ragozin, reached after 1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Nf3 Bb4, is a hybrid defence that grafts the Nimzo-Indian pin onto a classical Queen's Gambit Declined framework. By keeping the pawn on d5 while pinning the c3-knight, Black trades the passivity of the old QGD for active piece play and immediate pressure against White's centre.
line: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Nf3 Bb4

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: The defining feature of the Ragozin is the marriage of two respected systems: Black retains the ...d5 pawn that gives the Queen's Gambit Declined its solidity, yet develops the dark-squared bishop actively to b4 as in the Nimzo-Indian rather than passively to e7. The pin on the c3-knight strengthens Black's grip on the e4-square and discourages the immediate central expansion that would otherwise let White stamp his authority on the game. In return Black accepts that the bishop may later be exchanged for the knight, conceding the bishop pair but often saddling White with doubled c-pawns or a slightly loosened structure.

Pawn structures in the Ragozin are famously fluid. If the centre is liquidated after cxd5 and recaptures, an isolated queen's pawn frequently arises, and both sides must understand IQP play: White seeks piece activity and kingside chances, while Black blockades the d5-square and steers toward a favourable endgame. Alternatively White may release the tension early to reach a symmetrical, manoeuvring middlegame where the bishop pair yields a small but durable pull. Knowing when to allow doubled c-pawns, when to blockade, and when to open the position for the bishops is the essence of handling the line well.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: White's principal try is 5.cxd5 exd5 6.Bg5, renewing the pressure on the pinned knight and leading to Carlsbad-style manoeuvring, though here Black's bishop already sits actively on b4. A second major branch is 5.Qa4+, developing with tempo and inviting ...Nc6 or ...Nbd7, after which White hopes to unpin favourably; the closely related 5.Qb3 pursues the same idea. The quiet 5.Bg5 is also common, meeting the pin with a pin of its own and steering toward rich, tension-filled positions where both sides jockey for the central squares.

A well-known continuation runs 5.cxd5 exd5 6.Bg5 h6 7.Bh4 (or 7.Bxf6 Qxf6), after which Black completes development with ...O-O, ...Nbd7 and the freeing ...c5, striking at the centre and contesting White's spatial claims. In several lines an early ...dxc4 followed by ...c5 or ...b5 transposes toward accepted or Vienna-like structures, making the Ragozin's kinship with the Queen's Gambit Declined: Vienna especially clear, since both rest on the ...Bb4 pin combined with active central play. Precise move order matters, because a single careless tempo can hand White a comfortable, pressure-free edge.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The system is named after the Soviet grandmaster Viacheslav Ragozin, an analyst and correspondence world champion who championed the ...Bb4 idea from the 1930s and helped establish it as a fully respectable alternative to the classical Queen's Gambit Declined. Long viewed as a slightly offbeat sideline, the Ragozin was revitalised by modern grandmasters and deep computer analysis, which confirmed its soundness and flexibility; it has since appeared regularly at the very highest level as a reliable way for Black to fight for the initiative rather than merely equalise.

keyIdeas: Black keeps the ...d5 pawn of the QGD while adding a Nimzo-Indian pin with ...Bb4 against the c3-knight.
The pin fights for control of the e4-square and discourages White's immediate central expansion.
Exchanging the b4-bishop for the c3-knight can give White doubled c-pawns in return for the bishop pair.
Isolated-queen-pawn middlegames are common, so both sides must master blockade and piece activity.
A well-timed ...c5 break challenges White's centre and frees Black's position.
The line transposes naturally toward related ...Bb4 systems such as the QGD Vienna.

white: Play cxd5 and Bg5 to pressure the pinned knight and reach a favourable Carlsbad-type structure.
Use Qa4+ or Qb3 to develop with tempo and try to unpin the c3-knight on good terms.
Accept doubled c-pawns when the bishop pair and central control offer full compensation.
In isolated-pawn positions aim for the e3-e4 break, active pieces and kingside attacking chances.
Exchange pieces to convert the bishop pair into a small, durable endgame advantage.
black: Complete development with ...O-O and ...Nbd7 and prepare the freeing ...c5 break.
Maintain the ...Bb4 pin to restrain e4 and provoke structural concessions.
Trade on c3 at the right moment to inflict doubled pawns on White.
Blockade the d5-square and steer isolated-pawn positions toward a favourable endgame.
Use the active bishop and central pressure to seize the initiative rather than sit passively.
